items.title: Freshness SLAs by cadence, with an `ok | quiet | stale | broken` verdict
items.detail: Cadence is declared per source rather than one flat deadline for all of them: `CADENCE_DAYS` (src/freshness.js:101) gives each source a `cadence_days` and a `min_expected_delta`, so `noaa_enso` (35) and `who_gho` (730) are judged on their own publication clocks while the on-demand sources carry `cadence_days: null` and are given no deadline to miss. `explainVerdict` returns one of `ok | quiet | stale | broken | never_run` (src/freshness.js:64), and the four-way distinction is the item: a working source with nothing to report (`quiet`) and a dead source (`broken`) used to report the same string, which is how a healthy food-security pipeline and a broken one looked identical from the status route. The verdict reaches `GET /api/v1/ingest/status` as a `verdict` object beside the legacy `status` string (src/ingestion.js, src/server.js:1352), and `sourceHealth()` at src/server.js:536 — replacing rather than breaking, so existing consumers of `status` keep working.

items.title: Per-source data assertions with quarantine-on-fail
items.detail: Assertions are data, not code: `SOURCE_ASSERTIONS` declares per-source `required_fields`, `value_range`, `coordinate_bounds`, `monotonic_dates` and `min_count_vs_trailing` rules as frozen plain objects (src/assertions.js), so a test can read the map, count it, and require that nothing is declared without being measured. A batch that fails is withheld from its live collection and written to a `quarantine_<collection>` store instead, carrying the failures that condemned it (src/store.js, src/schema.js) — six quarantine collections, one per ingestable collection, with `test/ingestion-wiring.test.js` asserting the list covers `OUTPUT_COLLECTIONS` in both directions so a new collection cannot be added without either its quarantine home or a failure. The run reports `degraded` with the assertion text rather than the previous silent `store.merge`. Wiring this surfaced the falsy-zero trap twice in one afternoon: `Number.isFinite(Number(null))` is `true` because `Number(null) === 0`, so every null-valued field passes a `Number.isFinite` filter — the first fix appeared to work and did nothing, and it is now pinned by an explicit test. It also caught a defect in the guard rather than the data: the lite `conflict_csv` format has no identifier column, so requiring `source_id` quarantined 100% of documented uploads. The normalizer now mints one from the same fields the id is minted from and flags `source_id_minted` so nobody reads it as an upstream key.

items.title: Watermarks, incremental fetch, resumable backfill
items.detail: `src/watermarks.js` (27 tests) implements the per-source watermark, incremental fetch windows, resumable backfill cursors and the resume-after-crash case, but nothing calls it. The two archive connectors still default `endDate` to today and re-walk from 1981 on every run, and both still mint their record id from `endDate`, so a fresh id is minted daily and the whole backfill is re-downloaded forever. `gdacs-archive.js` remains a synchronous loop with no progress and no resume. This is the module-built-but-uncalled shape described under the patterns below: the logic is right and unreachable, and the work left is plumbing it into the three connectors.
items.note: src/watermarks.js is pure — state in, state out, nothing stored — and the connector contract already accepted and returned `options.watermark_state` / `output.watermark_state`. Nothing supplied either end, so a 40-year archive walked its whole series on every run and re-downloaded it to discover nothing was new. Now a declared collection, read once at the start of a run and written back only for sources that reported a position, so an interrupted run keeps its cursor instead of losing it. Backfills resume through `resumeBackfill` and report through `backfillProgress`. test/watermark-persistence.test.js: the second run resumes from what the first stored; an unwired connector keeps its position rather than resetting it; sources do not read each other's.

items.title: Source-agreement cross-validation
items.detail: `src/agreement.js` computes what the item asks for — Pearson and Spearman correlation with `minPearson: 0.5`, a paired-month count floor, a sign-disagreement rate capped at 0.25, and a four-value verdict of `agree | marginal | disputed | unavailable` — and it pairs on `period`, never on array index, which is the mistake that makes naive cross-product comparison meaningless. `unavailable` is returned rather than a fabricated verdict when either side is flat (`dx === 0 || dy === 0`), because a flat product carries no ordering information. Two things are missing: there is still no GeoTIFF reader (CHIRPS declines to decode pixels at src/connectors/chirps.js:23), so the two products cannot actually be compared in production; and no route surfaces `agreementReport` — the module is a library with no caller, which is the same defect ENH-16 has.
items.note: src/agreement.js. Coverage is its own axis with its own vocabulary, one-sided months named rather than counted: `unmatched_months` compared two sizes, so two products covering twelve disjoint months each differ by zero — a clean bill of health for a comparison that never happened. 'these two disagree' and 'only one covers this' no longer both arrive as `unavailable`. No winner is declared, by the spec's own words. test/source-trust.test.js.

items.title: Connector health scoring and circuit breaking
items.detail: The breaker is reached: `runIngestion` gates each source through `allowRequest` before it fetches, and an open circuit produces `status: 'skipped'` with `verdict` naming the reason — reported distinctly from `ok` and from `broken`, because a skip is not a success and not a failure, it is 'we did not look'. Failure streak was previously computed at src/ingestion.js and read nowhere else; it now opens the circuit after three consecutive failures, with a half-open probe and a cooldown. `src/circuit.js` also scores each source on latency, success rate and payload drift. Two things keep this partial: the breaker state is per-run, so it does not survive a process restart and a restarting poll loop still burns three failures every cycle; and the health score is computed but not surfaced on any route.
items.note: src/circuit.js. closed -> open on three consecutive failures -> half_open after the 30-minute cooldown -> exactly one probe, which closes or re-opens with the cooldown restarted. Recovery is asserted reachable in both directions; `opened_at: null` never probes. scoreConnector scores the breaker from STORED run history via outcomesFromRuns, not the in-memory window runIngestion rebuilds and discards per run — it previously existed only in tests. A breaker skip is not a success. test/connector-circuit.test.js.

items.title: Enforce the rate limits that are already declared
items.detail: Unchanged from before and still the item's own words: the token bucket, concurrency cap, jitter and `Retry-After` handling exist as `src/rate-limit.js` with 30 tests, and nothing enforces them. `src/connectors/http.js` is still plain exponential backoff, and the declared `rateLimit` fields — `src/connectors/ipc-hdx.js:417` declares perMinute 20 against the unbounded `Promise.all` at ipc-hdx.js:265 — remain documentation. The webhook branch of `distributeReport` still fetches with no timeout and no AbortSignal (src/server.js:1814-1819), and there is still no API rate limiter. Only the RapidPro client timeout from the previous round is actually live (src/rapidpro.js:370-379).
items.note: fetchWithRetry acquires from a per-source, per-host token bucket before every request (src/connectors/http.js), so the rateLimit blocks in the connector specs and connectors.registry.json stop being documentation. A headerless 429 now waits for whichever is longest of Retry-After, the bucket's next token, or the backoff — a 500 says nothing about anyone's rate budget, so only 429 consults the limiter. ratePerWindow and windowMs can be overridden per call, which is what makes a refill assertable without waiting out a 60-second window. test/rate-limit-wiring.test.js: bursting, per-host budgets, holding a budget across calls, releasing the slot when a request fails, and refusing an unreadable declaration rather than inventing a limit.

items.title: Raw payload retention, replay, and fixture seeding
items.detail: `src/capture.js` (27 tests) plus `scripts/capture-fixtures.mjs` implement raw-payload retention, content-addressed fixture seeding and replay: `withCapture` wraps a fetch, stores the body, and can serve it back so a connector test replays bytes instead of mocking `globalThis.fetch`. The fixture capture path exists and can be run. What does not exist is the call site: no connector is wrapped in `withCapture`, so nothing is actually retained in production and no fixture in test/fixtures/ was produced by the script — they remain hand-assembled, which is the reason the capture exists.
items.note: src/capture.js. RETENTION_POLICY states the window in one place and renders it into log lines, store files and the CLI's own output. Pruning leaves a tombstone that round-trips through the store file, and ReplayPrunedError is distinct from ReplayMissError: 'we captured it and policy took it' and 'we never captured it' are different facts. Every replay carries a provenance stamp with deliberately no `unstamp`. Replay through fetchWithRetry now carries tombstones too. test/capture-retention-replay.test.js, test/capture-cli.test.js.

items.title: Bitemporal records
items.detail: Every upstream-revisable collection now keeps the value it replaced. `mergeById` still overwrites by id — that is correct for the live set — but `JsonStore.merge` (src/store.js:124) now calls `supersededVersions` before the overwrite and merges the result into a new `record_versions` collection, so `valid_from`/`valid_to` intervals plus the previous body survive. `valueAsOf(collection, id, when)` reconstructs what the platform believed at a past instant, and `changedFields` names which fields moved. Two decisions worth stating. `NON_SEMANTIC_FIELDS` excludes `updated_at`, `ingested_at`, `generated_at` and `last_run_at`, because otherwise every daily re-ingest would report a revision and the history would be noise. And `versionRow` sets `payload_hash: null` deliberately: the body being stored is the predecessor's, and carrying the incoming hash would make `mergeById` drop the history row as a duplicate of the record it describes. A record with no timestamp at all produces no history row — the overwrite still happens, and the platform declines to lie about when.

items.title: Completeness tripwires for capped pagination
items.detail: `src/completeness.js` (26 tests) implements the pagination bookkeeping the item asks for: pages fetched, records seen, provider-declared total, whether the last page was full, and a `possibly_incomplete` flag when a cap bit before a floor rather than after one. Nothing calls it. `gdacs-archive` still walks quarter windows and keeps nothing about each page except the feature count, and `chirps` still applies its 30-record cap without recording what it dropped, so a truncated walk is indistinguishable from a quiet upstream — which is the entire finding.
items.note: The verdict is a run-record field, a scanned flag and a status-route verdict — read BEFORE the assertion pass can replace the output, because a quarantined batch drops every non-collection key, which is exactly when an operator most needs to know. test/pagination-completeness.test.js.

items.title: Record-level provenance with real transform versions
items.detail: All four defects this item listed are closed. `upstream_url_or_endpoint` is the URL actually fetched, not a constant null: `fetchWithRetry` records every fetch against the current run (src/connectors/http.js:18), which is the only place the retrieval URL is knowable at all, since no connector exposes the URLs it builds internally. `transform_version` is derived from the connector function's own body hash (`transformVersionFor`, src/provenance.js:112) and moves when the parser moves, rather than being the typed-in `'0.1.0'`. Each published record is stamped `_source_run_id` at ingest, and the lineage loop filters on it — previously it rebuilt a run-wide union inside the per-run iteration, so a nine-source run wrote nine identical rows each describing all nine. Provenance is read back from `record._source_run_id` rather than recomputed, so the attribution travels with the record instead of being re-derived from a set that has since changed.
